title: Breathing & Performance
description: How the engine breathes in and out through its induction and exhaust systems, and, as the course grows, how its performance is measured and what changes it.

sources.title: FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook - Powerplant, FAA-H-8083-32B (2023)
sources.applicability: Primary source for the general principles in this course. PDF page locators are used in step notes.

lessons.title: Induction & Exhaust
lessons.objective: Follow the air through the induction system and the burned gas through the exhaust: compare natural aspiration with supercharging and turbocharging, trace the GTSIO-520-H induction path, name the kinds of exhaust system, and recognise the hazards and inspections that go with them.
lessons.completionCriteria: Trace the air from the scoop to the cylinder and the gas from the cylinder to the tailpipe, say what drives a turbocharger and what a waste gate does, explain normalizing and critical altitude, and name three things to check on an exhaust system and why.

steps.title: Filling the cylinder
steps.prompt: A cylinder can burn only the oxygen that reaches it. As altitude increases and the air pressure falls, predict what happens to the mass of air a naturally aspirated cylinder of fixed volume can draw in. Then follow the air in through the induction system, and the burned gas out through the exhaust.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 133-142 and the glossary on PDF p. 476, supported by EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 205-216. The prediction is qualitative; no power-loss rate is given.

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt that sets up the whole lesson: charge mass depends on pressure.

steps.title: From scoop to cylinder
steps.prompt: Air is collected by a scoop in the cowling, passes an air filter, and reaches the fuel metering device, a carburettor or a fuel injector. The throttle plate controls how much air flows, and the pressure after it is the manifold pressure, measured in inches of mercury, which sets the power. An intake manifold with long curved pipes then carries the air, or the air-fuel mixture, to each cylinder. A balance tube evens out the pressure between the two sides so that every cylinder gets its share. On a fuel-injected engine the fuel is injected at the intake port just before the intake valve.
steps.alt: FAA exploded drawing of a downdraft balanced induction system: a throttle body, hoses, an induction manifold assembly, four intake manifold tubes and their intake gaskets, all labelled.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 129-130 (scoop, filter, fuel metering device, throttle and manifold pressure, balance tube; updraft and downdraft systems; fuel injected at the intake port), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 71-72 and 195-196. A general example, not a drawing of the GTSIO-520-H, whose induction system comes later in the lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: The labelled drawing shows the parts of a balanced intake manifold that the text names.

steps.title: The intake stroke
steps.prompt: At 90° of the cycle the piston is moving down and the intake valve is open, so the charge flows in. The thin coloured trace through the intake port is the model's gas cue: it shows the direction of flow, not a measured flow. Notice how little time there is: the intake valve is open for only part of the cycle, and the whole charge must pass the valve in that time.
steps.note: Documented four-stroke sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. The mechanism pose is profile-checked; the valve and gas cues are an ideal teaching profile, not GTSIO-520-H timing or CFD. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The shared 720-degree cylinder profile puts the learner at the intake stroke with the valve open.

steps.title: Dirt, ice and heat
steps.prompt: The induction system has three enemies. Dust is hard and abrasive, and an engine that breathes it wears its cylinder walls, rings and bearings, so the air passes a filter that must be cleaned or replaced on schedule. Ice can form in clouds, fog, rain or humid air, in three kinds: impact ice, fuel evaporation ice and throttle ice, and it can cut off the charge or change the air-fuel ratio. Carburettor heat takes warm air from around the exhaust to melt it, but warm air is less dense, so it reduces the weight of the charge and the power. Use it only as needed.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 131-132 (three types of induction icing; carburettor heat takes warm air from around the exhaust and reduces the weight of the charge and the power; dust damage and filter servicing), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 195-196. The handbook says on PDF p. 130 that carburettor heat leans the mixture and on PDF p. 131 that the mixture becomes richer, so this step does not state a direction.

mediaPlan.rationale: A maintenance-relevance step; the hazards are explained in words before the boosted systems.

steps.title: Driven supercharger
steps.prompt: Trace the mechanically driven supercharger from the crankshaft drive to the compressor impeller and the intake manifold. The compressor raises the density of the charge, but the engine itself has to supply the power to turn it. Compressing air also heats it, so some installations need to cool the charge before it reaches the cylinders.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of an internally driven supercharger induction system, with the intake air duct, carburettor heat valve, carburettor, supercharger, intake pipe and manifold pressure gauge labelled.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 133-135 (internally driven superchargers, mechanical drive, the charge gains heat as it is compressed). Figure 3-10 is the primary visual source.

mediaPlan.rationale: A real induction diagram makes the engine-driven compressor visible.

steps.title: Turbo energy path
steps.prompt: Open and close the waste gate, then trace the exhaust energy through the turbine and the compressor. Notice how the compressor discharge pressure, the pressure before the throttle (upper-deck pressure) and the manifold pressure are related, without treating them as identical at every operating condition.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 135-142 (a turbine driven by exhaust gas turns the compressor; the waste gate controls how much exhaust reaches the turbine). The animation explains control relationships qualitatively and does not calculate boost for a real engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: Opening and closing the waste gate makes the control relationship causal, not just labelled.

steps.title: Where the turbocharger sits
steps.prompt: This normalizing installation shows the whole layout in a nacelle. The exhaust from the cylinders is collected and carried to the turbocharger. The compressor air goes into the induction system and on to the intake manifold. Find the alternate air intake: if the air filter clogs, an alternate air door lets the compressor draw air from inside the cowling instead.
steps.alt: FAA cutaway of an engine nacelle with the air intake, alternate air intake, induction system, intake manifold, turbocharger, exhaust system, control system and the throttle and mixture control labelled.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 137 (the turbocharger air induction system consists of a filtered ram-air intake; an alternate air door within the nacelle admits alternate air if the filter clogs) and PDF p. 138 (Figure 3-16). A general example of a small-aircraft installation, not the GTSIO-520-H.

mediaPlan.rationale: A single cutaway shows where the induction and exhaust systems meet at the turbocharger.

steps.title: Normalize or boost
steps.prompt: A normalizing turbocharger makes up for the pressure lost with altitude, up to its critical altitude. It is not used to raise the manifold pressure above 30 inches of mercury. A ground-boosted (sea-level boosted) system can raise it above ambient, to around 40 inches, so the engine can develop more power at sea level than it could without the turbocharger. Critical altitude is the highest altitude, in a standard atmosphere, at which the system can still hold a chosen power or manifold pressure at a given engine speed. The handbook is careful to call only a ground-boosted system a true supercharger. Which kind an engine has depends on its installation and limits.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 133 (normalizing systems are not ground-boost systems and never boost above 30 inches; a true supercharger boosts manifold pressure above ambient), PDF p. 137 (normalizer turbocharger; ground-boosted systems raise manifold pressure above 30 inches to around 40 inches) and PDF p. 140 (the definition of critical altitude).

mediaPlan.rationale: A vocabulary step that keeps normalizing, ground boosting and critical altitude distinct.

steps.title: The GTSIO-520-H induction path
steps.prompt: The GTSIO-520-H is geared, turbocharged, fuel injected and has an intake air intercooler. Follow the numbered parts in the manual's figure: the turbocharger (3) feeds the air throttle (6), a duct (7) carries the air to the intercooler (14), and the intake manifold (17) shares it between the intake tubes (23), one to each cylinder. Compression heats the air a great deal: the handbook gives an example of up to 500 °F leaving a compressor on a 100 °F day, when the allowable air temperature at the throttle inlet is only about 230 to 300 °F. A cooler stops the charge getting close to detonation.
steps.alt: Continental manual figure C-3-2, an exploded drawing of the GTSIO-520-H induction system with the turbocharger, air throttle, air induction duct, intercooler, intake manifold and intake tubes numbered.
steps.credit: Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Figure C-3-2
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 152 (C-3-2: the engine is geared, turbocharged, fuel injected, with an intake air intercooler) and PDF p. 161 (Figure C-3-2, the -H induction system and its parts list), with the disassembly order on PDF p. 157. The flow order is read from the figure. The handbook (FAA-H-8083-32B, PDF p. 142) describes an aftercooler between the compressor and the air throttle inlet and gives the temperature figures; installations differ, so follow the manual for the engine in front of you.

mediaPlan.rationale: The manufacturer figure for the course engine names every part of its induction path.

steps.title: Altitude compare
steps.prompt: Move the altitude slider and switch between the naturally aspirated, normalizing and ground-boosted modes. Compare the ambient pressure with the manifold pressure each system can hold, and find the altitude beyond which a system can no longer reach its target.
steps.note: Documented relationships from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 133-142, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 205-216. The graph uses explicitly schematic values and is not performance data for any engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: Moving the altitude makes critical altitude something the learner finds, not just reads.

steps.title: Control and limits
steps.prompt: A turbocharger is controlled by its waste gate, which lets exhaust gas bypass the turbine. On many engines engine oil pressure moves the waste gate: more oil pressure closes it, more gas goes through the turbine and the boost rises. Two controllers share the work, one for full throttle and one for part throttle. Two terms are easy to confuse. Overboost is manifold pressure above the engine's limit, and it can cause serious damage. Bootstrapping is a slow drift of manifold pressure in the controls, which is not harmful to engine life. Limits and procedures come from the data for the installed engine.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 138-142 (waste gate position set by oil pressure in the actuator; density controller and differential pressure controller; overboost versus bootstrapping and overshoot; a pressure relief valve in some systems). This step explains purpose and vocabulary; it gives no operating limits or procedures.

mediaPlan.rationale: A vocabulary and control step; the numbers belong to the installed engine's data.

steps.title: The exhaust stroke
steps.prompt: At 630° the piston is moving up and the exhaust valve is open, pushing the burned gas out. The thin coloured trace through the exhaust port is the gas cue, again only a direction. The exhaust system's first job is to take this hot, poisonous gas away safely, and it also has to survive the heat, corrosion and vibration while doing it.
steps.note: Documented four-stroke sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48 and exhaust-system duty from PDF p. 149 (a scavenging system that collects and disposes of high-temperature, noxious gases safely). The valve and gas cues are an ideal teaching profile, not GTSIO-520-H timing or CFD. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The shared 720-degree profile puts the learner at the exhaust stroke with the exhaust valve open.

steps.title: Short stack or collector
steps.prompt: There are two kinds of exhaust system. A short stack (open) system lets each cylinder blow out through its own short pipe; it suits non-supercharged and low-power engines where noise does not matter. A collector system gathers the gas from the cylinders into collector tubes. It is used on most large non-supercharged engines and on all turbosupercharged engines, because on those the gas must be collected to drive the turbine. A collector raises the back pressure, the pressure the exhaust has to push against, but on a turbocharged engine the power gained is more than the power lost. The tapered ends of the collectors work as ejectors, drawing cooling air through the engine compartment.
steps.alt: FAA cutaway of a horizontally opposed engine in its nacelle, with red exhaust down-stacks joining collector tubes on each side that run aft to the exhaust ejectors at the firewall.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 149-150 (short stack and collector systems; collector systems on all turbosupercharged engines; back pressure and the turbosupercharging gain; exhaust ejectors and augmenter tube action), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF p. 72.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cutaway shows the stacks, collectors and ejectors in place in a nacelle.

steps.title: Radial collector ring
steps.prompt: A radial engine has its own pattern. Its collector ring is a welded, corrosion-resistant steel assembly made in sections, each section collecting the exhaust from two cylinders; on the 14-cylinder engine in the figure there are seven. The sections grow in size from the inboard side to the outboard side, where the tailpipe joins the ring. A telescoping expansion joint at the tailpipe lets a section of the ring be removed without taking the tailpipe off.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of the exhaust collector ring of a radial engine: a ring of welded sections joined to short stacks at each cylinder port, graduated in size towards the tailpipe connection.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 150 (radial engine exhaust collector ring: seven sections on a 14-cylinder engine, each collecting from two cylinders, graduated in size; telescoping expansion joint), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF p. 73.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook drawing shows the graduated sections of a collector ring.

steps.title: Mufflers and heat exchangers
steps.prompt: On many single-engine aircraft a shroud around part of the exhaust acts as a heat exchanger. It heats air for the cabin, for windscreen defrosting and for carburettor heat. That makes it a risk: about half of all muffler and heat-exchanger failures are cracks in the heat-exchanger surface, which let exhaust gas into the cabin heat system, a carbon monoxide hazard, or into the induction system, causing overheating and power loss. Inside a muffler, erosion and carbonisation can break baffles loose and block the flow. Blocked or restricted exhaust raises the back pressure and takes power away; backfiring and burning of unburned fuel in the exhaust make these failures more likely.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 149 (shroud heat for the inlet air, cabin heater and windshield defrosting), PDF pp. 151-152 (about half of muffler and heat-exchanger failures are cracks in the heat-exchanger surfaces; carbon monoxide; exhaust drawn into the induction system; internal baffle and diffuser failures restrict the flow and cause partial or complete power loss; backfiring and unburned fuel in the exhaust are contributing factors). Backfiring itself is covered in the Operation Malfunctions lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: The hazards are chains of cause and effect that read best as text.

steps.title: Inspecting the exhaust
steps.prompt: Any exhaust failure is a severe hazard: carbon monoxide in the cabin, loss of power, or fire. Inspect the clamped joints and port connections for leaks, which show as a flat grey or sooty black streak. Look at every weld, bend, clamp, support and gasket for cracks, dents and missing parts. A part that cannot be inspected where it is can be plugged, pressurised to about 2 psi and dipped in water, and any leak shows as bubbles. Never use galvanised or zinc-plated tools on an exhaust system and never mark its parts with a lead pencil: the lead or zinc enters the hot metal, softens it, and causes cracks.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of three types of exhaust system, labelled A, B and C, with red arrows marking the primary areas to inspect at joints, flanges, mufflers and heat-exchanger shrouds.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 150-151 (any exhaust failure is a severe hazard; no galvanised tools or lead pencil marks; leaks show as a flat gray or sooty black streak; inspection of welds, clamps, supports and gaskets; the 2 psi water test; Figure 3-42). This is a recognition lesson: the system manufacturer's data gives the limits and torques.

mediaPlan.rationale: The figure marks where each type of exhaust system is inspected.

steps.title: Turbocharged exhaust
steps.prompt: When there is a turbocharger the exhaust works under much higher pressure and temperature. At altitude the exhaust pressure is held near its sea-level value, so a small leak escapes with torch-like force and can damage nearby structure. Carbon (coke) deposits in the waste gate make it work erratically, and a waste gate that sticks closed causes overboost. Deposits in the turbocharger itself cause a slow loss of power. Periodic de-coking keeps the system efficient, and the cleaning and adjustment follow the manufacturer's instructions.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 152 (exhaust systems with a turbocharger: greatly increased pressure and temperature, torch-like leaks, coke deposits in the waste gate, waste gate sticking closed causing overboost, de-coking, manufacturer's instructions).

mediaPlan.rationale: A short maintenance step that connects the exhaust to the turbocharger control ideas.

steps.title: Breathing sets the power
steps.prompt: Trace the whole path in your own words: the scoop, filter and throttle, the intake manifold, the open intake valve, then the exhaust valve, collector and tailpipe, and where a turbocharger takes energy from the exhaust to raise the pressure of the induction air. How well an engine fills its cylinders is called volumetric efficiency, which the next lessons use. Then take the lesson's quiz.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner pulls the lesson together (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence). Volumetric efficiency is defined in FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 56, and used in the performance lessons.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner explains the path in their own words.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Power
lessons.objective: Explain why a piston engine's power changes: how altitude, temperature and humidity thin the air it breathes, and how ignition timing, spark plugs, fuel metering, induction and exhaust leaks, and low compression take power away.
lessons.completionCriteria: Sort the causes of a power loss into natural and mechanical factors, explain the effect of altitude, temperature and humidity on the oxygen each intake stroke draws in, and say what early or late ignition, a fouled plug, an induction or exhaust leak and a compression leak each do to the engine.

steps.title: An air breather
steps.prompt: A piston engine is an air breather. It takes in air, adds fuel, lights the charge and takes power from the expanding gas. So anything that changes the quality of the air, or the way the engine burns the charge, changes the power. Before you read on, list what you think can lower an engine's power. Then sort your list into two kinds: things nature changes, and things that can be wrong with the engine.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 37 (the typical aircraft engine is an "air breather"; anything that adversely impacts the quality of the atmosphere affects the power output; nature's variables and mechanical issues). The sort into natural and mechanical factors follows the module and the course deck (slides 229-239, 243).

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt that sets up the two groups of factors.

steps.title: Air available
steps.prompt: Change the altitude, the temperature compared with a standard day, and the humidity. Watch how much air is available to burn. Which of the three matters most? Which can you do nothing about? Then try the three example days.
steps.note: Built for this lesson from the standard atmosphere and the ideal-gas law (pressure and temperature at altitude; Charles's law as in EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 38-39; water vapour taking part of the pressure, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 39). "Air available" is the mass of dry air in the volume each intake stroke draws, as a fraction of a standard sea-level day. It is a teaching quantity, not a prediction of any engine's power.

mediaPlan.rationale: Three sliders make altitude, temperature and humidity something the learner changes and compares.

steps.title: Altitude and pressure
steps.prompt: As an aircraft climbs, the air pressure falls and the air gets thinner. It holds fewer molecules of oxygen in each unit of volume. A piston engine draws in the same volume of air on every intake stroke, whatever the altitude, so each stroke takes in less oxygen and the engine makes less power. The course rule of thumb is a loss of about 3% of the power for every 1,000 ft of climb in a naturally aspirated engine, which the interactive agrees with. A supercharged or turbocharged engine makes up the lost pressure up to its critical altitude.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 37-38 (ambient pressure falls with altitude; the air becomes rarified, with less oxygen per unit volume; each intake stroke ingests less oxygen at altitude, so the horsepower is reduced; an engine with no supercharging struggles at 15,000 ft). The 3% per 1,000 ft rule of thumb is from the course deck (slide 230) and agrees with the standard-atmosphere model used in the interactive (about 2.8% per 1,000 ft to 5,000 ft). Turbocharging is covered in Induction & Exhaust.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cause is one idea, said once, then explored in the interactive.

steps.title: Temperature
steps.prompt: Hot air is thinner than cold air. When air is heated at constant pressure its volume grows in proportion to its absolute temperature (Charles's law): 500 cu in of air at 0 °C becomes 500 × 323 ÷ 273 = 591.6 cu in at 50 °C. The engine still draws in the same volume, so the same intake stroke holds fewer oxygen molecules, and the power falls as the temperature rises. In an engine with a carburettor the mixture also becomes richer as the temperature rises, which lowers the power further.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 38-39 (Charles's law, V1 ÷ V2 = T1 ÷ T2 with the worked example of 500 cubic inches at 0 °C and 50 °C, absolute temperatures 273 and 323 K; a piston engine is a positive displacement pump, so the number of oxygen molecules entering falls as temperature rises; the mixture consumed enriches as temperature increases). Absolute temperature is the temperature in degrees Celsius plus 273.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short law with a worked number; the learner then sees it in the interactive.

steps.title: Humidity
steps.prompt: Air always carries some water vapour, and the vapour takes up room that oxygen would otherwise fill. When the humidity is high there is less oxygen per unit volume of air, so each intake stroke takes in less oxygen and the combustion of the charge is altered. The effect is small on its own: saturated air on a standard day holds about 2% less dry air. On a hot, humid day it adds to the effect of the heat, and the interactive shows a loss of about 10% at sea level.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 39 (high humidity means less oxygen per unit volume because of the space occupied by water vapour, so each intake stroke pulls in less oxygen). The figures are from the standard-atmosphere model in the interactive (Magnus formula for the vapour pressure): saturated air at 15 °C is 1.7% water vapour by pressure. The course deck (slide 233) gives a 1-3% loss.

mediaPlan.rationale: The effect and its size are stated once; the interactive shows how it combines with heat.

steps.title: Spark quality and timing
steps.prompt: A spark plug needs thousands of volts to make a hot spark, and the magneto makes them itself. If the contact breaker inside the magneto is timed wrongly, the spark is weaker and the charge burns less well. Separately, the spark has to arrive at the right moment. If it is too late (retarded), the charge is still burning as the piston passes TDC, so less of the heat reaches the piston, more goes out of the exhaust, the exhaust gas temperature rises and power is lost. If it is too early (advanced), the piston absorbs more heat than intended and the charge can detonate. In an extreme case the engine can fail.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 39-40 (magneto internal timing and the e-gap; retarded timing, heat lost through the exhaust, higher exhaust gas temperature and power loss; advanced timing, detonation and, in extreme cases, engine failure), and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48 (the ignition timing is the manufacturer's, 20° to 35° before TDC on various engines). The GTSIO-520 manual lists spark at 20° BTC for both magnetos (PDF p. 153). Timing procedures are in the manufacturer's data.

mediaPlan.rationale: Cause and effect of early and late timing read best as a short account tied to the earlier lesson.

steps.title: Spark plugs and leads
steps.prompt: The most common ignition fault is a fouled spark plug. Lead fouling is the usual kind, and it is most often found on the lower plugs: once the ceramic nose fills with lead deposit, the high voltage runs along the deposit instead of across the gap and the plug stops sparking. It shows at the pre-takeoff magneto check: the engine runs rough when the magneto that feeds the fouled plug is selected on its own. Faults on the secondary side, such as the coil, the carbon brush, the distributor rotor or the harness, make the cylinders they serve misfire and the engine run rough.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 40 (spark plug fouling, lead fouling most often on the lower plugs, found during the ignition system check before takeoff; secondary system faults cause roughness and misfiring). The magneto check is described in the accessories and maintenance lessons.

mediaPlan.rationale: A diagnostic story that connects a fault to a symptom the learner can recognise.

steps.title: Fuel metering
steps.prompt: The fuel metering system must mix fuel and air in the right proportion at the throttle setting the operator chooses, and the fuel must be broken into a fine spray so it mixes thoroughly. A wrong proportion changes the power. Typical faults: in a float carburettor, a faulty needle valve or a leaking float; in a continuous-flow fuel injection system, dirty nozzles, which cause roughness, or the wrong unmetered fuel pressure, which makes the cylinders get the wrong mixture. The GTSIO-520-H manual, for example, lists an unmetered fuel pressure of 6.0 psi at 450 propeller rpm. The adjustment has many steps and is done only from the manufacturer's data.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 40-41 (the fuel metering system must supply the right ratio and the fuel must be atomized; float carburettor defects; dirty nozzles in continuous-flow injection; incorrect unmetered fuel pressure in the Continental system) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 153 (C-3-3: unmetered fuel pressure 6.0 psi at 450 propeller rpm). The number is given as an example of the kind of value that has to be right and is not an instruction.

mediaPlan.rationale: The faults are a list the learner connects to the mixture; the example number comes from the course engine's manual.

steps.title: Leaks, heated air and rigging
steps.prompt: The gaskets and seals in the induction system leak with time. Any induction leak changes the fuel-air mixture the engine receives and costs power, so the system is inspected for leaks. Heated air does the same: if the carburettor heat control does not reach full cold, the engine breathes warmed air, the mixture is enriched and the performance falls, which is why the rpm drops when the pilot checks the heat. Control rigging matters too. Without full throttle travel the engine cannot make full power, and a controllable-pitch propeller that cannot reach the full-rpm position will not reach takeoff rpm.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 40-41 (induction leaks alter the fuel-air mixture and reduce power; the carburettor heat control not at full cold enriches the mixture and reduces performance; lack of full throttle travel or propeller control travel). Induction troubleshooting is also in FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 133 (Figure 3-8, air leaks and restricted ducts and filters). The handbook's statements on the direction of the mixture change with carburettor heat disagree (PDF pp. 130-131), so the direction is taken here only from the EASA text.

mediaPlan.rationale: The chain from a small leak or a short control travel to a loss of power reads best as text.

steps.title: Exhaust leaks and restrictions
steps.prompt: The exhaust is the other end of the breathing path. The gaskets at the exhaust ports are prone to leaking after a time in service, and a leak disturbs the flow of the exhaust leaving the port and so the flow of air and fuel into the cylinder. A leak in the carburettor heat system makes the engine breathe exhaust fumes when the heat is applied, and the rpm drops a lot. Leaks can also let carbon monoxide into the cabin. A blocked or restricted exhaust, such as a muffler with a broken baffle, keeps burned gas in the cylinder and costs power.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 41 (exhaust port gasket leaks; a leak in the carburettor heat system causes a large rpm loss when the heat is applied; carbon monoxide in the cabin) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 152 (internal muffler failures restrict the flow of exhaust gases and cause partial or complete power loss). The Induction & Exhaust lesson has the system and its inspection.

mediaPlan.rationale: The exhaust faults reuse the system from the previous lesson, so a short text is enough.

steps.title: Where compression leaks
steps.prompt: At 300° both valves are closed and the piston is squeezing the charge. For the power stroke to be strong, the charge must stay in. Find the three places it can leak: past the piston rings, between the valve faces and their seats, and through the cylinder wall if it is scored. Spotlighted here are the rings, the valves and the spark plugs.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 41 (cylinder compression is needed to extract the heat energy of the charge; the piston rings and cylinder walls wear and leak; the intake and exhaust valves may become leaky). The course deck (slide 243) adds a leaky head gasket. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The compression-stroke pose with the sealing parts spotlit shows where a cylinder can lose its charge.

steps.title: Finding a compression leak
steps.prompt: A differential compression test finds the leak. Air is fed into the cylinder, and where it escapes tells you the cause: air heard coming out of the intake system is passing a leaky intake valve, air coming from the exhaust pipe is passing an exhaust valve. A borescope can then be used to look inside. Hot gas rushing through a leak burns the carbon off the valve and discolours it at that spot. A leaking hydraulic lifter can also cost power, because it cannot hold the right valve lash and so reduces how high and how long the valve opens.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 41 (leaky valves found with the differential compression test, audible leaks from the intake system or the exhaust pipe, a borescopic inspection, discoloration of the valve at a leak; a leaky zero-lash lifter reduces the height and duration of valve opening). The test procedure and its limits are covered in the Maintenance and Servicing lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: The diagnostic reasoning is the content; the procedure itself belongs to the maintenance lesson.

steps.title: Sort the causes
steps.prompt: A naturally aspirated engine that is delivering less power than it should: take each of these in turn and decide whether nature or the engine is the cause, what you would check first, and why. High altitude on a hot day. A rough run on one magneto at the check. A big rpm drop when the carburettor heat is applied. A cylinder with air hissing from its exhaust pipe during a compression test. Then take the lesson's quiz.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner applies the factors to cases (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence) from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 37-41.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner works through cases in their own words.

checks.question: Using the GTSIO-520-H manual's figure, put these parts in the order the air passes through them.
checks.hint: Start at the part that raises the pressure and end at the part nearest the cylinders.
checks.rationale: In Figure C-3-2 the turbocharger feeds the air throttle, a duct leads to the intercooler, and the intake manifold shares the cooled air between the intake tubes, one to each cylinder.

checks.question: What drives the compressor of a turbocharger?
checks.hint: Follow the energy path on the exhaust side.
answers: A turbine turned by exhaust gas
A gear train from the crankshaft
The magneto drive
checks.rationale: Exhaust gas turns the turbine, which shares a shaft with the compressor impeller. A supercharger that is driven from the crankshaft is an internally driven supercharger, not a turbocharger.

checks.question: What does a normalizing turbocharger system do?
checks.hint: Compare the pressure it holds with the pressure outside as the aircraft climbs.
answers: Makes up the pressure lost with altitude, up to its critical altitude
Raises the manifold pressure above 30 inches of mercury at sea level
Cools the cylinder heads with the exhaust gas
checks.rationale: A normalizer regains the pressure lost as the aircraft climbs, up to its critical altitude. It is not used to boost manifold pressure above 30 inches of mercury; that is a ground-boosted system.

checks.question: What is the critical altitude of a turbocharged engine?
checks.hint: It is a limit on how high the system can keep its target.
answers: The highest altitude at which it can still hold a chosen power or manifold pressure at a given speed
The altitude at which the waste gate opens fully
The altitude at which the engine must be shut down
checks.rationale: Critical altitude is the maximum altitude, in a standard atmosphere, at which a specified power or manifold pressure can still be held at a specified speed. Above it the waste gate is fully closed and the manifold pressure falls.

checks.question: Match each part of a turbocharged induction and exhaust system to its job.
checks.hint: One part acts on the exhaust side and three on the air side.

pairs.right: Decides how much exhaust gas goes through the turbine
Raises the pressure of the incoming air
Cools the compressed air before it reaches the manifold
Stops dust and other matter entering the engine

checks.rationale: The waste gate sets the turbine speed by bypassing exhaust gas, the compressor raises the air pressure, the cooler takes out the heat of compression, and the filter protects the cylinders from abrasive dust.

checks.question: Which kind of exhaust system do all turbosupercharged engines use, and why?
checks.hint: The gas must be gathered in one place.
answers: A collector system, because the exhaust must be collected to drive the turbine
A short stack system, because it gives the lowest back pressure
No exhaust system, because the turbine lets the gas out directly
checks.rationale: On a turbosupercharged engine the exhaust gas has to be collected and carried to the turbine. A collector system raises the back pressure, but the gain from turbosupercharging is greater than the loss.

checks.question: How does an exhaust leak at a clamped joint show itself?
checks.hint: Look for a mark, not for a sound.
answers: As a flat grey or sooty black streak on the pipes near the leak
As a bright blue stain on the cowling
As frost on the collector tube
checks.rationale: An exhaust leak leaves a flat grey or sooty black streak around the joint. It is usually caused by poor alignment of two mated parts, which are repositioned to make a gas-tight fit.

checks.question: Why must exhaust parts never be marked with a lead pencil or worked with galvanised tools?
checks.hint: Think about what happens to the mark when the metal gets hot.
answers: The lead or zinc is absorbed by the hot metal, softens it and causes cracks
The marks make the part heavier
The tools would rust and block the pipes
checks.rationale: When the metal is heated the lead or zinc is absorbed, changing its structure and softening it in that area, which leads to cracks and eventual failure.

checks.question: A crack opens in the heat-exchanger surface of an exhaust muff that heats the cabin. What is the main hazard?
checks.hint: Exhaust gas is poisonous.
answers: Exhaust gas, with carbon monoxide, can reach the cabin
The cabin heater will make too much heat
The exhaust will become quieter
checks.rationale: A failure of the heat-exchanger surface lets exhaust gas into the cabin heat system, a carbon monoxide hazard. The gas can also be drawn into the induction system, causing overheating and power loss.

checks.question: What can happen when baffles inside a muffler break loose?
checks.hint: Think about the gas that needs to get out.
answers: They can block the exhaust flow and cause partial or complete loss of power
They make the engine run cooler
They only make the engine quieter
checks.rationale: Pieces of internal baffling that partly or fully block the flow restrict the exhaust and can cause partial or complete engine power loss. Erosion and carbonisation under extreme heat are the usual causes.

checks.question: What is overboost?
checks.hint: It is not the same as the manifold pressure drifting up and down.
answers: Manifold pressure above the limits set for the engine, which can cause serious damage
A slow drift of manifold pressure in the controls, which does no harm to the engine
The pressure of the exhaust gas at the turbine
checks.rationale: Overboost means exceeding the manifold pressure limit for the engine. The slow drift in the controls is bootstrapping, which is not harmful to engine life.

checks.question: Put the steps in the order that takes a naturally aspirated engine from a climb to a loss of power.
checks.hint: Start with the aircraft, end with the power.
items: The air pressure falls and the air gets thinner
Each intake stroke draws in fewer oxygen molecules
Less fuel can be burned and the power falls
checks.rationale: The engine draws in the same volume of air on every intake stroke, but thinner air holds fewer oxygen molecules per volume, so less fuel can be burned and the power falls.

checks.question: Match each factor to its effect on the engine.
checks.hint: Two of these come from nature and two from the engine.

pairs.right: Thinner air, so fewer oxygen molecules per intake stroke
The air expands, so each intake stroke holds less oxygen
The charge burns after TDC and more heat leaves through the exhaust
Risk of detonation and, in extreme cases, engine failure

checks.rationale: Altitude and temperature thin the air; retarded timing wastes heat through the exhaust and raises the exhaust gas temperature; advanced timing makes the piston absorb too much heat and the charge can detonate.

checks.question: 500 cubic inches of air at 0 °C is heated to 50 °C at the same pressure. What volume does it occupy?
checks.hint: Use absolute temperatures: add 273 to each Celsius temperature, then V2 = V1 × T2 ÷ T1.
checks.rationale: V2 = 500 × 323 ÷ 273 = 591.6 cu in. The engine still draws in the same volume, but this much air now holds the oxygen of the original 500 cu in, so each intake stroke takes in about 15% less.

checks.question: A naturally aspirated engine makes 200 hp at sea level. Using a loss of 3% of the sea-level power for each 1,000 ft, estimate its power at 5,000 ft.
checks.hint: Five thousand feet is five lots of 3%.
checks.rationale: Five lots of 3% is 15%, so the power is 85% of 200 hp, which is 170 hp. It is a rule of thumb for a naturally aspirated engine; real engines differ.

checks.question: Why does high humidity reduce engine power?
checks.hint: Think about what the water vapour takes the place of.
answers: Water vapour takes up space, so each intake stroke draws in less oxygen
Water makes the fuel heavier so it will not burn
Humid air is denser, which chokes the intake valve
checks.rationale: Water vapour occupies room that oxygen would otherwise fill, so there is less oxygen per unit volume and each intake stroke takes in less of it. The effect is small by itself but adds to heat.

checks.question: What happens to the exhaust gas temperature when the ignition timing is retarded?
checks.hint: Where does the heat go if the charge is still burning after TDC?
answers: It rises, because more of the heat leaves through the exhaust and less reaches the piston
It falls, because the charge burns more completely
It stays the same, because only the pressure changes
checks.rationale: With a retarded spark the charge keeps burning after the piston has passed TDC, so less heat is transferred to the piston, more is lost through the exhaust, the exhaust gas temperature rises and power is lost.

checks.question: At the pre-takeoff magneto check the engine runs rough on one magneto. What is a common cause?
checks.hint: It is the most common ignition fault, and it favours the lower plugs.
answers: Lead fouling of the spark plugs that magneto feeds
Too much fuel in the float bowl
A leaking exhaust gasket
checks.rationale: When the ceramic nose of a plug fills with lead the high voltage follows the deposit and not the gap, so the plug does not spark. Selecting the magneto that feeds it makes the engine run rough.

checks.question: The carburettor heat control does not reach full cold. What is the effect?
checks.hint: Warm air is thinner.
answers: The engine breathes warmed air, the mixture is enriched and the performance falls
The engine gets more oxygen and makes more power
The throttle travel increases
checks.rationale: Heated induction air enriches the fuel-air mixture and reduces engine performance. This is why the rpm falls when the pilot applies carburettor heat at the check.

checks.question: In a differential compression test, air is heard escaping from the exhaust pipe. Where is the leak?
checks.hint: The air goes out the way the burned gas normally leaves.
answers: Past the exhaust valve
Past the intake valve
Through the spark plug
checks.rationale: Air that escapes from the exhaust pipe is passing a leaky exhaust valve; air heard from the intake system is passing a leaky intake valve. A borescope can then be used to look at the valve.

checks.question: How can a leaking hydraulic lifter reduce engine power?
checks.hint: Think about the valve-train lesson.
answers: It cannot hold the right valve lash, which reduces the height and duration of the valve opening
It makes the camshaft turn at the wrong speed
It changes the firing order
checks.rationale: A zero-lash lifter that leaks cannot hold the correct valve lash, so the valve opens less far and for less time than the cam intends, and the engine breathes less well.
